title: Meet Andi: how we built Rappi’s customer experience agent on AgentOS
body_markdown:
#### From a stalled pilot to more than 350,000 users in four weeks. The decisions, the guardrails, the red team, and what surprised us the most.


It’s a Saturday night. Someone in Bogotá opens WhatsApp, writes to Rappi that a product is missing from the order that just arrived, and sends a photo. Two minutes later the case is closed: the order was verified, the photo was checked, the compensation was approved, and the refund is on its way. No human agent handled that exchange.


The one who answered is Andi, Rappi’s customer experience agent. Andi has been talking to real customers since mid-August. Today it serves more than 350,000 Pro Black users on WhatsApp across every country where Rappi operates, in Spanish, English, and Portuguese, and it resolves more than eight out of ten conversations end to end without a human. Next week it opens to every user inside the Rappi app.


Andi runs on AgentOS, the home-built platform our Platform AI team described a few weeks ago in[From Shadow Agents to Employee Agents](https://engineering.rappi.com/from-shadow-agents-to-employee-agents-how-we-build-autonomous-agents-at-rappi-644244ff4c3a) . That article mentions, almost in passing, that “Rappi’s user support agent on WhatsApp” lives on the same runtime as every internal agent. This is the story of that agent: why we chose to build it on our own platform instead of buying one, how it went from a blank prompt to real customers in two weeks, what protects it, and what we got wrong along the way.


It’s not a recipe. It’s how we did it.


### What we had before


Customer support at Rappi had automation long before it had an agent. We had deterministic flows, small rule-based bots that walked a customer through a menu, and a growing collection of scripts that handled one thing each. They worked, in the sense that they never surprised anyone. They also never understood anyone.


And for many situations we had something simpler than a bot: nothing. There was no channel where a customer could just say what happened in their own words. If your problem wasn’t in the menu, your problem didn’t exist for the system, and it ended up with a human agent, or it ended up nowhere.


The gap was obvious. A customer doesn’t think in menus. They think “half my order is missing and I already paid.” What we needed was something that could listen, look at the order, look at the evidence, decide, and act. In 2026 that is an agent.


### The pilot that didn’t move


Our first instinct was the same one every team has: buy it. The market is full of platforms that promise exactly this, and we evaluated many of them, paid and open source. We ran a pilot with one of them.


The pilot taught us three things. It was hard to operate: every change to behavior went through someone else’s release cycle. It was rigid: the platform had opinions about how a support conversation should go, and Rappi’s operation did not fit those opinions. And when something went wrong, we couldn’t see why: the traces we needed to understand a conversation were partial, or late, or not ours.


Weeks in, we had the feeling that we weren’t moving. That feeling is worth listening to.


Meanwhile, the Platform AI team had built AgentOS for a different purpose: internal agents, operations, data, engineering. Jonatan Ponzo and his team walked us through what the platform could do for a user-facing agent, and slowly the question flipped. Instead of “which vendor should we pick,” it became “why would we pay for a platform when we already have one that lives in our infrastructure, speaks to our tools, and is maintained by people two Slack messages away?”


The decisive argument, though, wasn’t technical. It was about the customer. A support solution starts from a customer’s problem, and a good one adapts to that customer: who they are, what they ordered, what happened to them before, which channel they prefer to use. We want Rappi to be there when a customer needs us, in the channel they choose, with the same quality of attention every time. In customer experience, that is the difference between a solution and a differentiator. And it is very hard to build on top of someone else’s platform, where knowing your customer means shipping their data out and personalizing means waiting for a roadmap.


The reasons that tipped the decision, in the order they mattered to us:


- **Knowing the customer.** On our own platform, every system that knows the customer is one connector away: their orders, their history, their account. The agent can treat each person as Rappi knows them, not as a ticket number. This is the part we have only started to use, and the one we’re most excited about.
- **Flexibility.** At the behavior layer, Andi is configured through a prompt and a set of skills. If the operation changes, we change the text. No ticket to a vendor.
- **Iteration speed.** A change to the agent is a save, not a deploy. The next conversation uses the new version. We would use this more than we imagined.
- **Traces.** Every turn, every tool call, every cost is recorded and inspectable by us, immediately.
- **It already lived in our infrastructure.** Same identity, same network, same tool gateway, same evals as every other Rappi agent. Nothing to integrate twice.
- **Cost model.** We pay for tokens. Not for tokens and a platform license on top.
- **The knowledge stays home.** Every lesson from every conversation becomes a change in an artifact we own.
- **What we don’t have, we build.** If the agent needs a capability that doesn’t exist yet, we write it: a skill, a tool, a connector. No feature request to a vendor, no waiting for someone else’s roadmap.


We stopped looking at vendors and started building.


### Two weeks to the first real conversation


We started at the end of July. Andi is one agent, not fifteen: a single specialist that identifies the customer’s order, understands what happened, classifies the case, and loads the playbook for that type of problem. Playbooks are AgentOS skills, one per case type: a missing product, an order that never arrived, a delay, a charge that doesn’t match, a question about a promotion. Adding a case type means writing one skill and one row in a table, not rebuilding the agent.


In the first week we had the agent reading real orders and real customer data in the development environment. In the second, the integration with our messaging infrastructure was live and Andi was talking to a trusted circle of customers over WhatsApp: about a hundred and fifty conversations a day, with the whole team watching the traces in real time.


That second week is where “iteration speed” stopped being a bullet point. On a single night the agent went through nine versions while we watched real conversations and fixed what we saw: a parameter the model was inventing because a skill asked for something the channel never sent, a turn that ran too many tools and got cut off by a gateway timeout, a rule that was correct in the playbook and wrong in the model’s reading of it. Each fix was a text change and a save. Each was live on the next message.


It was also where we learned the shape of a good turn. A conversation over WhatsApp has to answer fast. Long agentic turns that read everything before replying were correct and useless: the customer had already sent “hello?” again. We redesigned the playbooks around short turns, using the questions the agent has to ask anyway as natural cut points, and the first turn of the heaviest case type dropped from more than a minute to twenty seconds.


*Andi in AgentOS: one specialist agent, one skill per case type.*


### One brain, many channels


Andi is often described as “the WhatsApp bot.” It isn’t. Andi is the agent; WhatsApp is one door.


Two pieces of infrastructure that Rappi had built over the years made that possible. The first is the layer that receives messages from each channel, resolves who is writing and manages the session. The second is the conversation orchestrator, which decides what happens at each step of a support conversation and which system handles it. AgentOS was added to that orchestrator as one more provider, speaking A2A, the agent-to-agent protocol the platform already exposed. Andi never had to learn what WhatsApp is.


Before Andi, another AgentOS agent runs: Sentinel. Identity is the foundation of everything else, so we don’t leave it to a conversation. Whoever writes has to prove they own the account with a one-time code sent to the email and phone registered in Rappi. Only then does the conversation reach Andi, with the customer’s identity and country already resolved by the channel layer, outside the agent and independent of anything the customer typed. Andi never has to guess who it’s talking to, and no message can convince it otherwise. Whether you write from WhatsApp, the app or any channel we open next, we know it’s you.


The practical consequence is that the same brain, with the same playbooks, the same identity and the same traces, now reaches WhatsApp and next week reaches the app, and will reach social channels after that, without replicating a single piece of the architecture. The customer chooses the door. The attention on the other side is the same.


*One agent, many channels.*


### The agent that talks doesn’t hold the checkbook


There is a design decision in Andi that we would make again on day one.


Andi decides whether a case is eligible and what the customer needs. Andi does not decide how much money to give. Compensation amounts are decided by a separate system, our Policy Decision Maker, an agent of its own that applies Rappi’s compensation policies with the evidence in front of it and returns a decision. Inside that system another specialist looks at the photos customers send: whether an image was generated by AI, whether it’s a duplicate of one we have seen before, whether it actually shows what the customer is describing.


The agent exposed to the customer knows what happened. The agent that holds the policies knows what it’s worth. Neither can be talked into doing the other’s job, because neither has the other’s tools.


The tools themselves come from a support MCP maintained by our Support Tools team. When Andi launched it had nineteen of them. Seven weeks later it has forty-seven, and every batch we added removed a category of cases that used to end with a human: adjusting a debt left by a cancellation, proving a double charge with the actual transaction data instead of asking the customer for a bank screenshot, telling a customer not only that a refund was processed but when it will reach them. The agent didn’t get smarter each time. It got more hands.


### Guardrails, in layers


Everyone asks the same question about an agent that can move money: how do you keep it safe? Our answer has four layers, and only one of them is the prompt.


**The prompt.** The playbooks say what the agent may do, in what order, and what it must never confirm without evidence from a tool. Anything the customer writes is treated as the customer’s claim, never as data.


**The platform.** AgentOS gives each agent a whitelist of tools, a budget, and a full trace of every action. Andi can only call what we listed, and everything it calls is on record. And every tool it calls runs with the identity that the channel layer verified, not with one the agent chose.


**The channel.** Before a message reaches the agent, the channel layer applies its own gatekeeper: a system that recognizes abusive patterns across conversations and can warn or cut access without spending a single model call. Guardrails that live in the infrastructure can’t be argued with in a chat.


**The people.** Before the public launch, Rappi’s security team ran a red team exercise against Andi for several days. They found two things. One was a consistency issue in how compensations could be triggered; it was fixed in under two hours. The other was a way of encoding a message that nobody on the team had anticipated, and that got the agent to do something it shouldn’t have. We adjusted the prompt while the exercise was still running, with no deploy, and the next attempt failed. Then our engineering team closed the same door at the infrastructure level so it doesn’t depend on the prompt at all.


We had prepared for many things. We had not prepared for that one. That is what a red team is for.


### Evals are not a launch event


A red team is a moment. What keeps an agent honest between moments is evaluation that never stops, and that is a practice we hold for every agent at Rappi, not something we did once for Andi.


Every version of Andi goes through the same loop before and after it ships. Before: simulated conversations, run by simulator agents against the new version, covering the case types and the ways customers actually write. After: judges that score real sessions every day on the things that matter, whether the agent verified before it acted, whether it stayed inside its playbook, whether it resolved or escalated for the right reason. On top of that, people from the support team review samples of real conversations and leave signed evaluations, which is how we found the debugging rule we describe below and how we learned that a weekday and a weekend are different queues.


The evals system was built between Platform AI and our Support Automation Tools team, and it is the same one the internal agents use. An agent can get worse without crashing; it just starts answering a little less well. We don’t want to find that out from a complaint, or from the next red team. We want to find it out the same morning.


### Launch day


August 20. Ten thousand Pro Black users. Everyone on the team was in the same channel, watching the traces, ready for the thing that breaks. We had rehearsed rollbacks.


Nothing broke.


That was the surprise of the launch: not a number, but the absence of an incident. AgentOS held. The channel infrastructure held. The playbooks held. On August 26 we opened to 25,000 users. On September 4, to 100,000. Today Andi serves more than 350,000 Pro Black users on WhatsApp, and the next step is all of them: more than 300,000. Mid-September, Andi opens inside the app to every Rappi user.


*A real case, anonymized: identified, verified, compensated, closed.*


### What the numbers say, and what they don’t


More than eight out of ten conversations are handled entirely by Andi: no human, either by design or by technical necessity. The goal is above ninety-seven percent, and we are closer to the bottom of that road than the top.


The number we watch most closely is not the automation rate. It’s the cost of each conversation. As we scale from 150,000 users to every Pro Black user and then to every user in the app, the challenge is to bring the average cost per conversation down to ten cents or less, while resolving more. Short turns, tool whitelists, smart context loading, and the constant pruning of what the agent reads are all in service of that number.


And there’s a number we learned to distrust. Early in September we reported an escalation rate and then discovered that a third of the conversations in the denominator were customers who wrote their email, got greeted, and never wrote again. Counted correctly, escalations were much higher than we had said. Every improvement since then is measured against the honest denominator.


### What we got wrong


**We built a version on a day that wasn’t representative.** One iteration was tuned against a weekday, where most cases are about orders already delivered. The weekend is about orders in progress. That version fixed seven percent of the weekend’s escalations. It wasn’t a bad version; it was a version for a different queue.


**We let a debugging instruction reach production.** For a few hours a rule meant to help us understand handoffs was making the agent explain internal reasons to customers. We caught it in the traces. The lesson was not about that rule. It was that the prompt is code, and it needs the same discipline: versions, diffs, a checkpoint you can restore, and someone reading every change before it ships.


**We assumed business rules we should have asked about.** More than once an improvement was reverted because the person writing the playbook inferred a policy instead of confirming it with the people who own it. The fix was a habit: when in doubt, ask.


**We underestimated latency as a product feature.** A correct answer that arrives after the customer has given up is a wrong answer.


### What we learned


**Building beats buying when the thing you need is your own operation.** A support conversation at Rappi depends on Rappi’s orders, Rappi’s policies, Rappi’s tools. No vendor ships that. AgentOS let us keep the parts that are ours and reuse everything else.


**Iteration speed is a safety feature, not just a productivity one.** The red team finding was closed in minutes because a fix was a text change. The nine versions in one night were possible for the same reason.


**Separate the agent that talks from the agent that decides money.** It made the system safer and made each piece simpler.


**Know who you’re talking to before you talk.** Identity resolved outside the agent, with a code the customer has to hold, is what lets everything after it be flexible.


**One brain, many channels.** The investment in channel and orchestration infrastructure paid for itself the day we didn’t have to build a second agent for the app. And it’s what lets a customer get the same attention no matter where they write from.


**Evaluate continuously, or you’ll find out from a complaint.**


**Expect something to break, and celebrate when it doesn’t.** Then keep watching, because the bottleneck will move.


### What’s next


Three kinds of cases still end with a human more often than we’d like: orders in progress where the courier isn’t moving, cancellations of an active order, and accounts that can’t order or pay. Each needs a capability, not a better prompt: a tool that can act on a live order, a rule that says when the agent may cancel, a safe way to diagnose and lift a restriction. That is the queue for the next quarter, together with the app launch and the next channels.


And there is a bigger step behind those. Today Andi knows the case. The next thing it learns is the customer: how you order, what has happened to you before, how you prefer to be helped. Attention that is not only fast and correct but personal, the way a good human agent who already knows you would treat you. That is where the agent on our own platform stops being a cheaper way to do support and becomes a reason to choose Rappi. We’re just getting started on it.


Andi will keep learning the way it has so far: from its own conversations, with the traces open, the evals running and the team reading them.


### The people


Andi is the work of a team across Tech, Product, AI and the business, and of the teams that built the platform and the tools it stands on. Eugenio de la Rosa, VP of CX Support & Fraud. Andrés Cobos, VP of Tech CX Support. Andrés de las Casas, Product Director CX Support. María Fernanda Granada, Product Lead CX Support. Christian Parada, Engineering Manager CX Support. Manuela Rojas, Engineering Lead CX Support. Jonatan Muñoz, Wilson Tapia and Luis Felipe Cabezas, Software Engineers CX Support. Manuel Gruezo and the CX Support Tools team behind the Policy Decision Maker and the support MCP. Rappi’s Red Team. And the Platform AI team led by Jonatan Ponzo and Cristina Angel who built AgentOS and gave us the confidence to bet on it.


And beyond the names: every person in Customer Experience, Support Automation, Support Tools, Platform AI and Tech who read a trace, flagged a case, or answered a question at midnight. This is theirs.


If you are building a user-facing agent inside a company that already has a platform, our advice is short: look at what you already have before you look at what you can buy. It might be closer than you think.
